Densify COMPLETE (mid PHYS 372–mid-381): Cap. 6 title; names of the end; against Didymus and eternity philosophers; fire proper; starry heaven; substance vs qualities / renovation; timing unknown; rabbinic millennia; signs; pastoral use — Cap. 6 close. source_text: CAPUT SEXTUM, De hujus mundi fine. A statu animae separatae sequitur hujus mundi finis, quo caeli (Enchir. c. 91.) non a causa naturali, sed ex determinatione libera & omnipotentia creatoris sui cum stridore praeteribunt; elementa aestuantia solventur, terraque & quae in ea sunt opera exurentur.
english: CHAPTER SIX. On the end of this world.

From the state of the separated soul there follows the end of this world, by which the heavens (Enchiridion chapter 91) will pass away with a great noise not from a natural cause but from the free determination and omnipotence of their Creator; the elements burning with heat will be dissolved, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.

source_text: V. Cum hic mundus cum omnibus bonis suis brevi interiturus, quietem ac tranquillitatem perpetuam animo nostro largiri nequeat, extrema vesania atque miseriae est, ei ita adhaerere, ut ejus amore verum bonum amittas; Christianae vero sapientiae & felicitatis est, in hac vita mundo ejusque bonis nuntium mittere, ut post hanc aeterno bono fruaris. Huc spectat monitio Pauli, 1.Cor. 7.29.30.31. & Davidis, Psal. 49.4.7.12.13.15.20.21.
english: V. Since this world with all its goods will soon perish and cannot grant perpetual quiet and tranquillity to our mind, it is extreme madness and misery so to cling to it that by love of it you lose the true good; but it belongs to Christian wisdom and felicity in this life to send a farewell to the world and its goods, so that after this life you may enjoy the eternal good. Hither looks Paul's warning (1 Corinthians 7:29, 30, 31) and David's (Psalm 49:4, 7, 12, 13, 15, 20, 21).

source_text: Frustra igitur sunt Mathematici quidam & philosophi, qui dicunt, fore eam anno magno, intra quem sol, luna & sidera cuncta ad eundem caeli locum, unde profecta sunt, remeant; de quo vide Censorinum de die natali cap. 18. Incertis quoque subnixa videtur conjecturis Judaeorum & quorundam patrum opinio, mundum duraturum sex annorum millibus: duobus ante legem, duobus sub lege, duobus post legem sub Messia. Quod dictum esse Eliae Thisbitae, non a Judaeis solum, sed Christianorum multis creditum est, uti Stratonico Cumano episcopo, quemadmodum ex collectaneis ejus probat Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. bibl. in Helias, qui & ipse ejus sententiae fuisse videtur, atque etiam Ludovicus Vives in lib. 20. de C.D. cap. 7. Nos Eliae quidem esse fatemur, at non Thisbitae, sed Rabbini Cabbalistae, cujus commentum, ut Genebrardus observat initio Chronographiae, legitur in Talmud, tractatu Sanhedrin & in tract. de idololatria & in tract. de sabbato.
english: Therefore certain mathematicians and philosophers are in vain who say that it will be in the great year, within which the sun, moon, and all the stars return to the same place of heaven whence they set out; on which see Censorinus On the Birthday chapter 18. The opinion of the Jews and of certain fathers also seems propped on uncertain conjectures — that the world will last six thousand years: two before the law, two under the law, two after the law under the Messiah. That this was said by Elijah the Tishbite has been believed not only by Jews but by many of the Christians, as by Stratonicus bishop of Cumae, as Sixtus of Siena proves from his collectanea (Sacred Library book 2, under Elias), who himself also seems to have been of that sentence, and also Ludovicus Vives (City of God book 20, chapter 7).

We confess indeed that it is Elijah's — but not the Tishbite's, but a Cabbalist Rabbi's, whose comment, as Genebrard observes at the start of his Chronography, is read in the Talmud, in the treatise Sanhedrin and in the treatise On Idolatry and in the treatise On the Sabbath.

source_text: Dissentiumt ab omnibus istis quidam juniorum, nominatim Johannes Chassanis, Theologus Gallus, Loc. Com. lib. 3. cap. 22. Cui sententiae favere videtur Apoc. 20.14. & 21.1. ubi disertim dicitur, mare non fore amplius; Psal. 102.27.28. Luc. 21.33. Jobi 14.12. Psal. 72.7. Hacpropter neque horum sententiam praefracte rejicere audemus, qui mundum secundum substantiam periturum esse arbitrantur: praesertim cum nihil de eo antiquitus synodo ulla sit definitum & quidam praestantes sane viri de eo dissentiant. Interim priorem sententiam magis probamus.
english: Certain of the juniors dissent from all these, namely Johannes Chassanis, a French theologian (Common Places book 3, chapter 22). Revelation 20:14 and 21:1 seem to favor his sentence, where it is expressly said that the sea will be no more; also Psalm 102:27–28; Luke 21:33; Job 14:12; Psalm 72:7. For this reason we dare not reject harshly the sentence of those who judge that the world will perish according to substance — especially since nothing about it was defined of old by any synod, and certain truly outstanding men dissent about it. Meanwhile we more approve the former sentence.

source_text: Rationes, quibus Rabbini veritatem hujus dicti propugnant, Rabbi Isaac in cap. 1. Geneseos quatuor affert. 1. quia primus Gen. versus sexies continet א, quo millenarius denotatur. 2. quia sex diebus fecit Deus caelum & terram, ac septimo quievit; mille vero anni coram Deo sint, sicut dies una. 3. quia Deus, tam in diebus quam annis, senario quidem laboris, septenario autem indicat quietis tempus. Nam sex diebus operari, septimo autem ab omni opere vacare nos jussit: idem etiam sexennium indulsit agriculturae, septimo vero anno, tam agro quam cultori, requiem indixit. 4. quia sex primi factores generis humani mortui sunt: nempe Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Jared: Enoch autem, qui septimus est, in locum Deo cognitum feliciter translatus, adhuc vivit. Quibus rationibus aliquot juniorum addunt: 5. quia corrupto genere humano dixerit Deus, Gen. 6.3. Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in aeternum, quia caro est: eruntque dies illius centum viginti annorum. Ubi primo intelligunt tempus poenitentiae concessum ante diluvium, quod fuit CXX. si quinquagies sumas, resultat numerus sex millium. 6. Etiam ex aetate Mosis idem colligunt. Nam vixit annos CXX. Deut. 34.7. ac quadraginta quidem annos in aula Pharaonis, Act. 7.23. item quadraginta annos in exilio apud Jethronem, Exod. 2.15. & 3.1. quibus adumbrantur bis mille anni sub lege: item quadraginta annos populum Israeliticum in deserto rexit, Exod. 16.35. quibus significantur bis mille anni sub imperio Messiae. 7. His addunt, quod arca Noachi requierit mense septimo, Gen. 8.4. quod Moses sex diebus fuit in nube, Exod. 24.16. septimoque vocatus a Domino; quod cum Israelitae, ex praecepto Domini, sex diebus circumiissent Jericho, septima die muri ejus corruerunt, Jos. 6.16. atque id contigit cum populus deserto egressus jam terram promissionis occupare inciperet: item quod angelus praedixit Esrae, 4.Esd. 7.30. saeculum fore septem dierum; praeterea quod septem tubae, Apoc. 8.2. septemque phialae Apoc. 16.1. commemorentur, & quaedam alia ejusdem generis. Quare quod praesentibus Apostolis dixit Christus, id nobis etiam dictum putemus: Non est vestrum nosse tempora, quae Pater in sua posuit potestate.
english: The reasons by which the Rabbis defend the truth of this saying, Rabbi Isaac on Genesis chapter 1 offers four. (1) Because the first verse of Genesis contains א six times, by which a thousand is denoted. (2) Because God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh; but a thousand years before God are as one day. (3) Because God, both in days and in years, indicates by the sixfold the time of labor and by the sevenfold the time of rest. For he commanded us to work six days and on the seventh to rest from all work: he also granted a six-year period to agriculture, but in the seventh year enjoined rest both on the field and on the cultivator. (4) Because the six first makers of the human race died — namely Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared — but Enoch, who is the seventh, happily translated into a place known to God, still lives.

To which reasons some of the juniors add: (5) Because when the human race was corrupted God said (Genesis 6:3), My spirit will not remain in man forever, for he is flesh: and his days will be one hundred twenty years — where first they understand the time of repentance granted before the flood, which was 120; if you take it fifty times, the number of six thousand results. (6) They also gather the same from Moses' age. For he lived 120 years (Deuteronomy 34:7): forty years in Pharaoh's court (Acts 7:23), forty in exile with Jethro (Exodus 2:15 and 3:1), by which two thousand years under the law are adumbrated; likewise he ruled the Israelite people forty years in the desert (Exodus 16:35), by which two thousand years under Messiah's empire are signified. (7) To these they add that Noah's ark rested in the seventh month (Genesis 8:4); that Moses was in the cloud six days and on the seventh was called by the Lord (Exodus 24:16); that when the Israelites had gone around Jericho six days, on the seventh day its walls fell (Joshua 6:16); likewise that the angel foretold to Esdras (4 Esdras 7:30) that the age would be of seven days; further that seven trumpets (Revelation 8:2) and seven bowls (Revelation 16:1) are commemorated, and certain other things of the same kind. Therefore what Christ said to the Apostles present, let us think said also to us: It is not yours to know the times which the Father has put in his own power (Acts 1:7).

source_text: III. Neque magis hominibus certum est, quando definite ac precise haec mundi conflagratio sit futura, ut, securitate excussa, semper sese ad eam parent vigilando, orando & poenitentiae exercitia obeundo. Nam sapienter Augustinus lib. 18. de C.D. cap. 53. Importune, ait, omnino illud quaeri. Et addit: Si hoc nobis nosse prodesset, a quo melius quam ab ipso Dei magistro, interrogantibus discipulis, diceretur? Non enim siluerunt inde apud eum, sed a praesente quaesiverunt, dicentes, Domine, si hoc in tempore restaurabis regnum Israel? At ille, Non est, inquit, vestrum nosse tempora quae Pater in sua posuit potestate. Non utique illi de die vel hora vel anno, sed de tempore interrogaverant, quando illud accepere responsum. Sic & Anastasius Sinaites lib. 7. Hexaem. tom. 1. bibl. patrum: Verum, inquit, exitum & finem saeculi solus scit creator temporum & universorum. Et Vincentius Burgundus in Speculo natur. lib. 32. cap. 102: Quantum temporis usque ad finem saeculi supersit, certum est neminem mortalem esse qui noverit, nisi forsitan Dominus alicui speciali gratia revelaverit. Omnium namque de hac re calculantium digitos quiescere jubet, qui ait: Non est vestrum nosse &c.
english: III. Nor is it more certain to humans when this world's conflagration will definitely and precisely be future, so that, security shaken off, they may always prepare themselves for it by watching, praying, and performing the exercises of repentance.

For wisely Augustine (City of God book 18, chapter 53): It is altogether importune, he says, that that be asked. And he adds: If it were profitable for us to know this, by whom better than by God's own Master would it be said to the asking disciples? For they were not silent about it before him, but asked of him present, saying, Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? But he: It is not yours, he says, to know the times which the Father has put in his own power (Acts 1:6–7). They had certainly not asked about day or hour or year, but about the time, when they received that answer. So also Anastasius of Sinai (Hexaemeron book 7): The true exit and end of the age, he says, only the creator of times and of all things knows. And Vincent of Beauvais (Natural Mirror book 32, chapter 102): How much time remains until the end of the age, it is certain that no mortal knows, unless perhaps the Lord has revealed it to someone by special grace. For he who says It is not yours to know commands the fingers of all who calculate about this matter to rest.

source_text: Posterioris notae sunt in mundi machina, in qua tum caelum spectatur, tum terrae marisque globus, Luc. 21.25.26. Vide Joh. Driedonem lib. 3. de scripturis & Eccles. dogm. tract. 3. fol. 159. Judaei tradunt quindecim signa, quae quindecim diebus praecessura sint diem novissimum, quae ex Hieronymo recenset Thomas lib. 4. sentent. dist. 48. q.1. a.4. Quod vero singulis signis suum praefiniunt diem, id Rabbinicum est. Huc quoque referunt, quod apparebit in caelo signum crucis, idque colligunt ex Matth. 24.30. Remaclus de Vaulx in Harpocrate divino sive de consummatione mundi parte 2. Hoc, inquit, signo crucem Christi significari, tam Graeci quam Latini, consentientibus animis asseverant. Et Lucas Pinellus de altera vita & animarum in ea statu lib. 2. cap. 20. Per hoc signum, inquit, Filii hominis crucem significari, omnes affirmant interpretes, tam Graeci quam Latini. Quos refellit Maldonatus in cap. 24. Matth. Simplicius videtur, si signum filii hominis ipse intelligatur filius hominis veniens in nube, Luc. 21.27. cujus conspectus certissimum erit signum finis mundi. Simili phrasi signum circumcisionis pro circumcisione ipsa accipitur, Rom. 4.11. Vide antiquitatis & eruditionis oceanum Gerh. Joh. Vossium disp. de adventu Christi, thes. 5.6.7.8.9.
english: Of the latter mark are things in the world's machine, in which both heaven is beheld and the globe of earth and sea (Luke 21:25–26). See Johannes Driedo On the Scriptures and Ecclesiastical Dogmas book 3, tractate 3, folio 159. The Jews hand down fifteen signs which will precede the last day by fifteen days, which Thomas recounts from Jerome (Sentences book 4, distinction 48, question 1, article 4). But that they assign to each sign its own day is Rabbinic.

Hither they also refer that the sign of the cross will appear in heaven, and they gather that from Matthew 24:30. Remaclus de Vaulx in Divine Harpocrates or On the Consummation of the World part 2: By this sign, he says, both Greeks and Latins with consenting minds assert that Christ's cross is signified. And Lucas Pinellus On the Other Life book 2, chapter 20: By this sign of the Son of Man, he says, all interpreters, both Greek and Latin, affirm that the cross is signified. Whom Maldonatus refutes on Matthew chapter 24. It seems simpler if the sign of the Son of Man is understood as the Son of Man himself coming in a cloud (Luke 21:27), whose sight will be the most certain sign of the world's end. By a similar phrase the sign of circumcision is taken for circumcision itself (Romans 4:11). See the ocean of antiquity and learning, Gerhard Johann Vossius, disputation On the Advent of Christ, theses 5–9.

source_text: II. Utrum vere hic mundus, quantum ad substantiam, an vero duntaxat quantum ad qualitates suas, interiturus sit, incertum est. Communior sententia est, mundum non simpliciter periturum, sed esse renovandum, impenseque hanc suadet Paulus Rom. 8.19.20.21.22. & quod caeli novi, terraeque novae in scripturis saepe sit mentio. Veteres, quorum sententias quasi per saturam colligit diffusae eruditionis vir Gerh. Vossius, cujus hic vitula aramus, disp. de fine mundi thes. 3. pag. 280. omnes putarunt, mundum hunc non penitus interiturum, sed esse renovandum, ut Irenaeus, Andreas Caesariensis, Probus apud Epiphanium, Eusebius, Philastrius, Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, Chrysostomus, Cyrillus Alexandrinus, Theodoretus, Aeneas Gazeus, Elias Cretensis in orat. 10. Greg. Nazianz. Basilius Imp. Constant. Oecumenius, Euthymius. E Latinis Hilarius, Hieronymus, Quintus Julius Hilarianus, Augustinus, Julianus Toletanus, Beda, Alcuinus, Ambrosius Ansbertus, Olympiodorus, Haymo, Anselmus sive Hervaeus Brito, Petrus Lombardus, Otto Frisingensis, Hugo Aetherianus, Hildegardis, Vincentius Burgundus, Nicolaus Liranus, Ludolphus Saxo Carthusianus &c.
english: II. Whether this world will truly perish as to substance, or only as to its qualities, is uncertain. The more common sentence is that the world will not simply perish but is to be renewed, and Paul strongly urges this (Romans 8:19, 20, 21, 22), and because new heavens and a new earth are often mentioned in the Scriptures.

The ancients, whose sentences Gerhard Vossius, a man of diffuse learning — whose heifer we plow here — gathers as it were in a medley (disputation On the End of the World, thesis 3, page 280), all thought that this world will not utterly perish but is to be renewed: as Irenaeus, Andrew of Caesarea, Probus in Epiphanius, Eusebius, Philastrius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Aeneas of Gaza, Elias of Crete on Gregory of Nazianzus's tenth oration, Basil the emperor Constantine, Oecumenius, Euthymius. From the Latins: Hilary, Jerome, Quintus Julius Hilarianus, Augustine, Julian of Toledo, Bede, Alcuin, Ambrosius Ansbertus, Olympiodorus, Haymo, Anselm or Hervaeus Brito, Peter Lombard, Otto of Freising, Hugh Etherianus, Hildegard, Vincent of Beauvais, Nicholas of Lyra, Ludolph the Saxon Carthusian, and others.

source_text: Dissentit Augustinus lib. 20. de C.D. cap. 24. & dubie loquens in psal. 101. Sunt, inquit, tres caeli caelorum superiores in firmamento. Sed utrum & ipsi perituri sint igni, an hi soli caeli qui etiam diluvio perierunt, disceptatio est aliquanto scrupulosior inter doctos; nec facile, maxime in angustia temporis, explicari potest. Quam multi vero nunc Augustini sequantur sententiam, Sixtus Senensis ostendit lib. 6. bibl. sanct. annot. 246. & Feuardentius in Irenaeum lib. 4. cap. 6. Quibus oppones patres tum Graecos universos, tum Latinos, qui ante Augustinum scripserunt, nominatim Justinum Martyrem, sive quemcunque alium in confut. dogm. Aristotelis lib. 2. de caelo neganti caelos posse corrumpi, Irenaeum lib. 4. cap. 6. Ambrosium lib. 1. Hexaem. cap. 6. & e junioribusque Augustinum Eugubinum in 2.Pet. 3. & Hieronymum Magium lib. 2. de exustione mundi cap. 6. & 7.
english: Augustine dissents (City of God book 20, chapter 24), and speaking doubtfully on Psalm 101: There are, he says, three heavens of heavens superior in the firmament. But whether they themselves also will perish by fire, or only those heavens which also perished in the flood, is a somewhat more scrupulous debate among the learned; nor can it easily be explained, especially in the narrowness of time. But how many now follow Augustine's sentence, Sixtus of Siena shows (Sacred Library book 6, annotation 246) and Feuardentius on Irenaeus book 4, chapter 6.

Against whom you will set the fathers, both all the Greeks and the Latins who wrote before Augustine — namely Justin Martyr, or whoever else, in the Confutation of Aristotle's Dogmas book 2 On the Heavens denying that the heavens can be corrupted; Irenaeus book 4, chapter 6; Ambrose Hexaemeron book 1, chapter 6; and among juniors also Augustinus Eugubinus on 2 Peter 3; and Hieronymus Magius On the Burning of the World book 2, chapters 6 and 7.

source_text: Ignis vero per metaphoram pro ira & judicio divino accipi putatur a Francisco Puccio Filidino, ut notat Nicolaus Serarius Jesuita Moguntinus lib. 1. contra Puccium cap. 2. & lib. 2. cap. 2. sed proprie sumi, argumento est, quod dicatur, ut aqua prius interiit, ita in illo die igne periturum. Hinc Augustinus lib. 20. de C.D. cap. 16. Tunc, inquit, figura hujus mundi mundanorum ignium conflagratione praeteribit: sicut factum est mundanarum aquarum inundatione diluvii. Quis vero ille ignis sit futurus & unde venturus, disputat Hieronymus Magius lib. 3. de exustione mundi: at nos Augustini modestiam amamus, qui loco laudato, neminem, quod ipse sciat, novisse haec arbitratur. Est vero hic controversum, an etiam caelum sidereum igne sit expurgandum? Antiquissimi patres id affirmant. Negat Augustinus, & cum eo juniores. Nos antiquiorum sententiam dictis scripturae, quibus mundum hunc periturum esse jam probavimus, nixam, altera potiorem ducimus.
english: But fire is thought to be taken by metaphor for divine wrath and judgment by Franciscus Puccius of Filidino, as Nicolaus Serarius the Mainz Jesuit notes (book 1 against Puccius, chapter 2, and book 2, chapter 2): yet that it is taken properly is argued by this, that it is said that as it formerly perished by water, so on that day it will perish by fire. Hence Augustine (City of God book 20, chapter 16): Then, he says, the figure of this world will pass away by the conflagration of worldly fires, just as it was done by the inundation of worldly waters in the flood.

But what that fire will be and whence it will come, Hieronymus Magius disputes in On the Burning of the World book 3: yet we love Augustine's modesty, who in the place praised judges that no one, so far as he himself knows, has known these things. But here it is controverted whether the starry heaven also is to be purged by fire. The most ancient fathers affirm it. Augustine denies it, and with him the juniors. We hold the ancients' sentence, resting on the sayings of Scripture by which we have already proved that this world will perish, to be preferable to the other.

source_text: Dicitur συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος consummatio saeculi hujus, Matth. 13.40. & 18.20. τέλος finis, Matth. 24.6.14. Messis, Matth. 13.39. & Apoc. 14.15.16. & Joel. 3.13. Mundus hic, ut initium habuit, ita & habiturus est finem, Apoc. 21.1. 2.Pet. 3.5.6.7.8.12. Neque hic probandus est Didymus, enarratione in epistolas canonicas, observans triplicis hic mundi mentionem fieri, antiqui seu praeteriti v.6. praesentis v.7. & futuri post hunc v.13. Quae huic epistolae adspersa putat ab haereticis, plures mundorum creationes & periodos somniantibus. Sed haec conjectura eum fefellit. Nam quod Petrus diluvio periisse mundum dicit, satis indicat, non loqui eum de tribus mundis τῇ οὐσίᾳ essentia diversis, ut Origenistae putarunt, sed illud solum indigitare, quemadmodum hic mundus semel coepit, & aqua corruptus fuit, ita eundem aliquando periturum igni.
english: It is called συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος, the consummation of this age (Matthew 13:40 and 18:20); τέλος, end (Matthew 24:6, 14); harvest (Matthew 13:39 and Revelation 14:15–16 and Joel 3:13). This world, as it had a beginning, so also will have an end (Revelation 21:1; 2 Peter 3:5, 6, 7, 8, 12).

Nor is Didymus to be approved here, in his exposition on the canonical epistles, observing that mention is made here of a threefold world — of the ancient or past (verse 6), of the present (verse 7), and of the future after this one (verse 13) — which things he thinks were sprinkled into this epistle by heretics dreaming of several creations and periods of worlds. But this conjecture deceived him. For that Peter says the world perished by the flood sufficiently indicates that he is not speaking of three worlds diverse in essence, as the Origenists thought, but only pointing out that just as this world once began and was corrupted by water, so the same will sometime perish by fire.

source_text: IV. Indefinitum vero tempus extremi diei Deus in scriptura revelavit, idque ab nostra hac aetate non usque adeo remotum esse varia significant. Alia declarant simpliciter adventum Christi appropinquare; alia vero cum adventu Christi sunt immediate conjuncta. Prioris notae sunt: 1. conversio Judaeorum praedicta Rom. 11.25. Apoc. 3.9. & 7.4.5.6.7.8. Vide Finum Hadrianum in Judaeorum flagello lib. 7. cap. 20. 2. praedicatio Euangelii per universum orbem, ut vult Augustinus epist. 78. & 80. ad Hesychium, Hieronymus in Matth. cap. 24. Origenes tract. 28. in Matth. Prosper resp. ad 4. cap. Gallorum. Ambrosius lib. 10. in Lucam. Auctor operis imperfecti homil. 48. in Matth. Damascenus lib. 4. de orthod. fide cap. 27. E recentioribus Liranus, Cajetanus, Maldonatus in cap. 24. Matth. Bellarminus lib. 3. de Rom. pontif. cap. 4. Suarez disp. 50. tom. 2.
english: IV. But God has revealed in Scripture an indefinite time of the last day, and various things signify that it is not so very remote from this our age. Some declare simply that Christ's advent is approaching; others are immediately joined with Christ's advent. Of the former mark are: (1) the conversion of the Jews predicted (Romans 11:25; Revelation 3:9 and 7:4–8) — see Finus Hadrianus in The Scourge of the Jews book 7, chapter 20; (2) the preaching of the Gospel through the whole world, as Augustine wills (letters 78 and 80 to Hesychius), Jerome on Matthew chapter 24, Origen tractate 28 on Matthew, Prosper's reply to the fourth chapter of the Gauls, Ambrose on Luke book 10, the author of the Incomplete Work homily 48 on Matthew, Damascene On the Orthodox Faith book 4, chapter 27. From the more recent: Lyra, Cajetan, Maldonatus on Matthew 24, Bellarmine On the Roman Pontiff book 3, chapter 4, Suarez disputation 50, tome 2.

source_text: Et sane semper hoc dogma in confesso apud Christianos fuit, quos idcirco deridet Porphyrius, teste Augustino lib. 20. de C.D. cap. 24. Platonem secutus, qui in Timaeo tradit mundum coepisse, at non interiturum. Alii etiam longius recesserunt, ut Xenophanes, qui nec coepisse, nec desituram mundum putabat, ut auctor est Plutarchus de placitis philosophorum lib. 2. cap. 4, idque longe ante Platonem. Vixit enim Xenophanes circa olympiadem 60. hoc est, Cyri & Tarquinii Superbi temporibus. Hanc Xenophanis sententiam magno nisu tuetur Aristoteles 8. auscult. & libris de caelo. Aristotelem mordicus defendit Averroes disp. 1. de aeternitate mundi, ubi Algazelis solutionibus respondet.
english: And indeed this dogma has always been among the things confessed among Christians, whom therefore Porphyry mocks, as Augustine witnesses (City of God book 20, chapter 24), following Plato, who in the Timaeus hands down that the world began but will not perish. Others also withdrew further, as Xenophanes, who thought the world neither began nor will cease, as Plutarch is author in On the Opinions of the Philosophers book 2, chapter 4, and that long before Plato. For Xenophanes lived around the sixtieth Olympiad, that is, in the times of Cyrus and Tarquinius Superbus. Aristotle with great effort defends this sentence of Xenophanes (Physics book 8 and On the Heavens). Averroes defends Aristotle tooth and nail in his first disputation On the Eternity of the World, where he answers Algazel's solutions.
